source_read: PDF (old scan), pp. 253-263, all 11 pages read on the rendered page (150 dpi); Figures 1 and 4 also at 300 dpi; every number below checked on the image, not the text layer

claims.overstatement: Minor: the statement says the vessels differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold 'for each drug'. That holds for every drug taken in overdose and for the metabolites (3.6 to 6.25), but lidocaine, given intravenously in hospital in Case 4, varied only 1.6-fold, and the authors say several-fold differences occur 'for some, but not all drugs' (p. 260). The magnitude does report lidocaine 1.6; 'for each drug taken in the overdose' would match the source exactly. Otherwise the wording is careful: it presents the case selection, the authors' explanation as theirs, and the before-death caveat.
claims.note: Pounder & Jones part of the claim only. Every number recomputed: doxepin 12.5/3.6 = 3.47; amobarbital 25.8/4.3 = 6.00; secobarbital 25.3/3.9 = 6.49; pentobarbital 31.5/5.1 = 6.18; clomipramine 21.5/4.0 = 5.38; flurazepam 0.99/0.15 = 6.60; imipramine 18.1/4.1 = 4.41; lidocaine 1.4/0.9 = 1.56; imipramine after death against the sample from life 4.1/2.3 = 1.78 and 18.1/2.3 = 7.87. All match the claim. The 'about 1 to 2 hours' is right: the text says the sample was drawn on admission about 1 h before cardiac arrest, while the stated timings (autopsy 9.25 h after the sample and 7.25 h after death) imply 2 h. The sample from life was drawn on admission, before gastric lavage. Continued absorption between that sample and death therefore cannot be excluded, which the claim's general caveat ('part of the differences may have arisen before death') covers. The 'lower after death' direction in the claim does not come from this source: all drugs here were higher centrally, and the only comparison with life shows higher post-mortem values.

anchors.locator: Abstract; affiliations; Materials and Methods, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Detailed human case data are presented to illustrate the extent of redistribution. Suspected overdose cases were identified before medico-legal autopsy, and multiple blood samples were taken by needle puncture of vessels after ligation or cross-clamping. Authors from Forensic Medicine, Dundee, and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, Edmonton. Neither the office the cases came from nor the years are stated. Four cases; each body was sampled at one autopsy.

Blood ranges across vessels, mg/L: Case 1 doxepin 3.6-12.5 (9 vessels), desmethyldoxepin 1.2-7.5. Case 2 amobarbital 4.3-25.8, secobarbital 3.9-25.3, pentobarbital 5.1-31.5 (11 vessels). Case 3 clomipramine 4.0-21.5 (10 vessels; mixed cardiac blood 15.3), flurazepam 0.15-0.99 (mixed cardiac 0.51). Case 4 imipramine 4.1-18.1 (11 vessels), lidocaine (given intravenously in hospital) 0.9-1.4. Highest/lowest per drug (editors' recalculation): 3.47, 6.00, 6.49, 6.18, 5.38, 6.60, 4.41; lidocaine 1.56; metabolites 3.6-6.25.

Highest values: pulmonary vein (Cases 1 and 4), supra-renal inferior vena cava (Case 2), pulmonary artery and vein (Case 3, clomipramine), infra-renal inferior vena cava (Case 3, flurazepam). Lowest: femoral or subclavian veins in Cases 2-4. In Case 1 the lowest doxepin was in the pulmonary artery (3.6 mg/L), and the femoral vein (about 5.0 mg/L on Fig. 1) was among the higher values.

Imipramine overdose treated in hospital with gastric lavage with charcoal and intravenous lidocaine. Ante-mortem blood drawn on admission, about 1 h before cardiac arrest; autopsy 9.25 h after that sample and 7.25 h after death (so about 2 h from sample to death). Ante-mortem imipramine 2.3 mg/L (desipramine 0.6; lidocaine not detected); post-mortem 4.1-18.1 mg/L, i.e. 1.78- to 7.87-fold (editors' calculation). The femoral veins read about 4.9 and 5.6 mg/L on Fig. 4 (about 2.1-2.4-fold); the subclavian veins were lowest.

Unabsorbed drug was in the gut in 3 of 4 cases. Case 1: tablet debris and two intact capsules in the duodenum. Case 2: stomach 746, 993 and 903 mg of the three barbiturates plus small-bowel amounts. Case 3: stomach 2,400 mg clomipramine plus small bowel; the authors call it substantial unabsorbed drug. Autopsy timing: Case 1 17 h after discovery and 40 h after last seen alive; Case 2 about 36 h after death; Case 3 about 24-48 h; Case 4 7.25 h.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 1st-5th paragraphs (p. 260 1st paragraph; p. 261 1st, 3rd, 5th; p. 262 continuation)
anchors.extracted: Several-fold differences occur for some, but not all, drugs. They are judged too large to be fully explained by incomplete distribution in life, although arterio-venous differences may contribute. Post-mortem diffusion from solid organs (liver, lung) into blood is proposed as the main factor, with the cause unresolved and probably multifactorial. An autopsy blood level may miss the level at death by several-fold, and an artefactually raised level in someone taking therapeutic doses may be misread as a lethal overdose. Databases of post-mortem levels without the sampling site are undermined.

Accurate, but it compresses one concession. The authors say arterio-venous differences from incomplete distribution are insufficient to account for the differences while conceding that they may contribute (p. 261, top paragraph continued from p. 260). That concession bears on the claim's caveat that part of the difference may have arisen before death.

reporting_issues.note: Abstract p. 253 against Fig. 1 p. 255: in Case 1 the pulmonary artery is lowest and the femoral vein is among the higher sites.
Independently seen at 300 dpi: no desmethyldoxepin bar is below about 1.5 mg/L. 7.5/1.5 = 5.0 against 7.5/1.2 = 6.25.
Methods (p. 254) give a desalkylflurazepam assay with no result reported, and no method for lidocaine or trichloroethanol.
p. 259: about 1 h before cardiac arrest, against 9.25 - 7.25 = 2 h. The sample was also drawn on admission, before the gastric lavage.
Case 2 has no stated cause or manner; Cases 1, 3 and 4 are called suicidal overdoses.

risk_of_bias.note: I agree with the overall 'high' and with each domain. METHODS §5.3 lists case series under 'no instrument', so the use of the JBI prevalence checklist rests on the first readers' round brief, which I have not seen. The overall judgment would be the same either way.

interpretation_gap.note: I agree it is 'minor'. The untested alternative of uneven distribution in life during ongoing absorption, and ref. 14 being a conference paper, are the right points.

missed: p. 260, Discussion, 1st paragraph: the authors themselves limit the several-fold differences to 'some, but not all drugs'. This bears on the claim's 'for each drug' (lidocaine varied 1.6-fold) and on 'vary between drugs'.

p. 261, top paragraph (continued from p. 260): the authors concede that arterio-venous differences from incomplete distribution may be a contributory factor. The card's key finding 7 gives only the rejection half.
